about.title: Fremont Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Fremont is a city of more than 232,000 people, and most of them spend their days moving through spaces someone else controls: shopping centers along Fremont Boulevard, office campuses, apartment complexes, restaurants, and the lots that serve them. When a property owner or manager lets a hazard sit, a routine errand can end with a fractured wrist or a head injury. California premises liability law asks a specific question in these cases: did the owner know, or should they reasonably have known, about the condition, and did they fail to fix it or warn about it? Answering that question is where claims are won or lost. Photos of the spill, the torn carpet, or the missing handrail matter, as do the names of anyone who saw it happen. Store and parking-lot cameras in Fremont often overwrite footage within days, so a prompt written request to preserve video can be decisive. Alameda County claims generally carry a two-year filing deadline, but falls on public property face a far shorter window. LawProactive can put you in touch with an independent attorney who understands these steps, free of charge.

whyChoose.title: Why Fremont Fall Victims Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: Attorneys who focus on the notice question
items.desc: California requires proof that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. Network attorneys know how to look for inspection logs, prior complaints, and maintenance records that show what a Fremont property manager was aware of and when.

items.title: Fast action on video and evidence
items.desc: Surveillance footage from a Fremont store or garage can be gone in days. Getting connected quickly means a preservation letter can go out before the recording is overwritten.

items.title: Clear guidance on deadlines and shared fault
items.desc: Most claims must be filed within two years, but a fall on city or county property triggers a much shorter government-claim process. Because California applies pure comparative fault, an attorney can also push back when an owner tries to shift blame onto you.

items.question: I slipped in a store on Fremont Boulevard and the manager said I wasn't paying attention. Do I still have a claim?
items.answer: Possibly. California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you are found partly responsible, you can still recover compensation reduced by your share of fault rather than losing the claim entirely. The bigger issue is whether the store knew or should have known about the spill and failed to clean it up or put out a warning. An attorney can request the store's sweep logs and camera footage to establish that.

items.question: What if I fell on a sidewalk or in a park owned by the City of Fremont or Alameda County?
items.answer: Claims against public entities follow a separate procedure with a much shorter deadline than the usual two years, and missing it can end the case before it starts. You generally must file a formal government claim first and wait for a response before going to court. Because of that timing, it is wise to speak with an attorney as soon as you can.

items.question: Does LawProactive charge me anything to get connected with a lawyer?
items.answer: No. LawProactive is a free service and is not a law firm; we connect you with an independent attorney in our network. Those attorneys handle premises liability cases on contingency, meaning you pay no attorney fee unless there is a recovery in your case.
